newsitem.title: USA: U.S. gives thumbs up to news of IMF-Thailand talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. gives thumbs up to news of IMF-Thailand talks.

text.p: News of talks between Thailand and the International Monetary Fund received the thumbs-up in Washington on Monday, where concern has mounted that a Thai cash crunch is hurting nearby states.

"We welcome the dialogue between Thailand and the International Monetary Fund as a constructive step and will be following it closely," U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said in response to questions.
"The United States has a strong stake in financial stability and growth throughout the developing world."

Thai officials, admitting for the first time that they were ready to consider asking for an IMF loan, said on Monday that they were in talks with a team from the fund to work out how to tackle a financial crisis and liquidity problems.
The crisis has already hurt economies in the region.

The Philippines, forced to devalue the peso soon after Thailand devalued the baht, has won $1.1 billion of emergency funding from the IMF, and other regional currencies have faced speculative pressure.
But the southeast Asian currencies recovered somewhat on Monday on news of the IMF talks.
An IMF spokesman said a team from the fund had already arrived in Bangkok. "An IMF team arrived in Thailand over the weekend and has initiated policy discussions with Thai officials," he said.
But monetary source said it was too early to predict the likely outcome of the talks or say how much money could be on offer if Thailand agreed to swallow IMF reform recipes.
"The team will be there for as long as is neccessary, but we are pretty much in the dark right now. We do not know exactly what the situation is," said one source.

A deal between Thailand and the IMF could open the door to a big multi-lateral support package on the lines of that extended to Mexico in 1995. Some analysts have said Thailand could need up to $20 billion.

Monetary officials had admitted they were worried about the possible implications of the Thai currency crisis on other emerging markets, although they said the problems were not as severe as those in Mexico in 1995.
"They will have to come to the IMF sooner or later," one official said late last week. "We only hope it is sooner, because it is later the problems will be bigger and harder to resolve."
Thailand last had a programme with the International Monetary Fund in 1985.
IMF First Deputy Managing Director Stanley Fischer said last week that Thailand needed measures on tax, currencies and banking, regardless of whether it had a programme with the IMF.
